video_title: Lawfare Daily: How Our Growing Software Dependence Threatens National Security
gist: Soufan Center researchers Colin Clark and Chad Sarena unpack their report 'Closing the Gap: Software Understanding in US National Security', arguing that the ability to verify and reason about software has been outpaced by its deployment, creating national-security risk that AI is now widening on the offense side faster than on defense. They highlight two under-appreciated risk dimensions — 'enured blindness' (ubiquitous cameras/mics/IoT that adversaries exploit for free, as Israel did in Tehran and Russia in Ukraine) and 'the tactical becomes the strategic' (industrial control systems compromised at scale) — and flag NDAA-mandated DARPA formal-methods transition, ONCD/CISA coordination and public-private partnership as the emerging policy response.

themes.theme: The software understanding gap as a named policy category

insights.claim: The 'software understanding gap' is defined as the ability to understand, verify and reason about software being dramatically outpaced by software's production, uptake and implementation, and the gap is still widening rather than closing.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: A newly-named risk category with a report, workshop lineage and legislative hook is the leading indicator of future federal procurement requirements for software assurance and verification tooling.
insights.quote: that's our ability to, the way we've explained it, to understand, to verify, um, to reason about software, which has been, you know, dramatically outpaced by its production and uptake

insights.claim: The speakers identify artificial intelligence as the newest factor exacerbating the software understanding gap, on top of the pre-existing growth in software prevalence.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Ties AI adoption directly to a growing verification deficit — supportive of demand for AI-assisted code analysis, formal verification and assurance vendors.
insights.quote: The newest monkey wrench is is artificial intelligence and and how we can see that.

insights.claim: The concept is so new that when the researchers polled security-community contacts about software understanding, most had no answer and did not recognize the terminology, meaning the field has been confined to technically gifted specialists rather than policy and security professionals.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Early-stage policy concepts with no shared vocabulary usually precede a multi-year build-out of standards, budget lines and consulting demand — an early positioning window.
insights.quote: a lot of people just didn't have an answer for us. They didn't know what the terminology meant.

insights.claim: The policy lineage runs from a 2023 Sandia Laboratories workshop in New Mexico, to an Office of the National Cyber Director 'Back to the Building Blocks' report, to a June 2025 Sandia-led 'closing the software understanding gap' report with NSA, OUSD(R&E) and DARPA interagency buy-in.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena and Colin Clark, Soufan Center
insights.so_what: Names the specific agencies and documents that will drive any resulting requirements — the map for where software-assurance contract dollars would flow.

insights.claim: The software understanding problem is framed as spanning both software quality and user comprehension, with a radical gap between what CTOs and software engineers understand and what ordinary civilian users — whose smart thermostats and refrigerators connect back to broader IT infrastructure — understand.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Frames consumer IoT as a national-security attack surface, the classic precursor to device-security labelling regimes and consumer-hardware compliance costs.

themes.theme: Enured blindness: adversaries riding free on our own sensor build-out

insights.claim: 'Enured blindness' is the report's term for the fact that societies have stopped noticing the cameras, microphones, doorbells and traffic cams that would have stood out like a sore thumb 20 to 40 years ago, which is itself now a security failure mode.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: A named risk dimension in a report circulating on Capitol Hill; watch for it to be cited in future rules on camera/sensor procurement and siting.

insights.claim: Civilian camera and sensor networks have already been operationally exploited by multiple actors: Israel tapped cameras across Tehran for pattern-of-life monitoring, Russia tracked logistics hubs and train stations in Ukraine, cartels tapped systems to track people, and Hamas used similar systems for collection.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Confirms sensor-network compromise is a proven, repeatedly used technique — raising the odds of regulation on camera supply chains and of demand for sensor-network hardening.

insights.claim: Ubiquitous consumer and municipal sensors have collapsed the cost of espionage from the Cold War model of inserting an expensively trained professional into a country to simply accessing infrastructure the target already paid for and installed.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Cheaper collection means more actors can do it, including low-resource ones — expands the addressable threat set for counter-surveillance and TSCM-style services.
insights.quote: I just have to access them and make sure you don't catch me accessing them.

insights.claim: Exposure to sensor-network exploitation scales with device density, making the United States likely the leading target and the United Kingdom — with heavy surveillance coverage in London and other English cities — also highly exposed, while sparsely equipped countries face materially less risk.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Implies the security-spend burden falls disproportionately on the most digitized economies — a structural tailwind for US/UK physical-and-cyber security budgets.

themes.theme: Pre-positioning and supply-chain intrusion as the dominant adversary pattern

insights.claim: The scale and complexity of software-defined systems underpinning US national security lets adversaries hide intrusions for extended periods and act at a time and place of their choosing before defenders even know a breach occurred.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Detection-dwell-time, not prevention, is the framed weak point — favors continuous monitoring, threat-hunting and asset-discovery vendors over perimeter tools.

insights.claim: SolarWinds is used as the canonical supply-chain case: Russian-injected malicious code in third-party software updates reached thousands of government agencies and private companies and went undetected for nearly a year, with the intelligence gained still unknown.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Keeps third-party update pipelines at the center of policy attention — SBOM, code-signing and vendor-attestation requirements remain the likely regulatory instruments.
insights.quote: third-party software updates distributed to thousands of government agencies and private companies and it went undetected for nearly a year

insights.claim: Intrusions into apparently benign civilian targets such as water plants in random parts of the United States may be dry runs — the functional equivalent of a weapons test to measure how long an actor can persist undetected before replicating the technique elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Reframes small-utility breaches as strategic reconnaissance, strengthening the case for federal mandates and funding reaching small municipal water and utility operators.
insights.quote: Civilian targets, water plants in, you know, random parts of the United States. What's the purpose of that?

insights.claim: China's Volt Typhoon pre-positioning inside US utilities and transportation hubs is read not as an attempt at immediate disruption but as a precursor to a future attack, most plausibly tied to a Taiwan contingency.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Links critical-infrastructure cyber risk to the Taiwan timeline — a scenario trigger for both defense-cyber spend and utility/transport operational risk.
insights.quote: it's hard not to think of a Taiwan scenario, some kind of a future Taiwan scenario

insights.claim: The same pre-positioning capabilities are expected to proliferate into non-US interstate rivalries such as India-Pakistan, Israel-Iran and Turkey, and to appear there in the near rather than distant future.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Widens the geography of infrastructure-cyber risk beyond US-China, relevant to sovereign risk and to cyber-insurance exposure in emerging markets.

themes.theme: When tactical incidents aggregate into strategic ones

insights.claim: 'The tactical becomes the strategic' is the argument that a single compromised industrial control system — like the Iranian-attributed attack on the system in Ellwood City, Pennsylvania — is a local tactical problem, but software-defined ICS penetrated at scale could disrupt thousands of water treatment facilities simultaneously and become a strategic event.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Scale-multiplication of commodity ICS attacks is the mechanism that turns a diffuse OT-security market into a national-priority spend category.
insights.quote: now that simple tactical problem becomes a strategic issue if these things were to be manipulated at scale or simultaneously.

insights.claim: Airports are cited as a parallel cascade vector: interfering with airport computer or communication systems grounds aircraft at multiple locations at once, and the failure compounds as people and logistics stop moving.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Aviation IT is framed as a low-effort, high-cascade target — relevant to airline operational-risk disclosure and to aviation-sector cyber requirements.

insights.claim: Cascading infrastructure failures can come from software simply not performing correctly, not only from attack, and it is often difficult to determine after the fact whether an event such as the Aliquippa water treatment disruption or Iranian gas-station pump hacks was deliberate or accidental.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Attribution ambiguity complicates cyber-insurance war exclusions and incident-disclosure obligations — a live coverage-dispute risk for insurers and operators.

themes.theme: Policy response: NDAA formal methods, ONCD, CISA and public-private partnership

insights.claim: Last year's National Defense Authorization Act directs the Department of Defense to develop a comprehensive strategy for transitioning DARPA's formal methods research investments into production environments across the department.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Cedarbaum, host
insights.so_what: A statutory mandate moving formal verification from research to production is a concrete, near-term procurement channel for verification-tooling and assurance contractors.
insights.quote: a comprehensive strategy for transitioning DARPA's formal methods research investments into production environments across the department.

insights.claim: The guests treat the NDAA formal-methods language as 'putting our money where our mouth is' while explicitly cautioning that formal methods is not a be-all end-all and that closing some vulnerabilities will surface new ones.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations of a one-shot fix — implies recurring, not one-time, assurance spending.

insights.claim: Software understanding is described as one of the rare areas of current bipartisan agreement on Capitol Hill, based on the researchers' recent direct conversations with lawmakers.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Bipartisan support raises the probability that software-assurance mandates survive political turnover — lower legislative risk on this spending theme than on most cyber policy.
insights.quote: I've spent some time recently on Capitol Hill talking to lawmakers about this

insights.claim: The guests argue the response must be organized through CISA and interagency cooperation with a public-private partnership, because a slow, piecemeal state-by-state legal approach across a country of 330 million leaves defenders perpetually behind the curve.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Signals a push toward federal-level coordination and industry co-option rather than state patchwork — watch CISA authorities and funding as the implementation vehicle.
insights.quote: you're you're going to be perpetually behind the curve if you're trying to very slowly and piecemeal establish laws

themes.theme: AI asymmetry and the uplift of non-state actors

insights.claim: AI accelerates both vulnerability discovery and remediation, but because attackers need only one exploitable flaw while defenders must identify and remediate all of them, AI confers a structural advantage on the attacker.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: If the offense-defense balance tilts, expect faster growth in incident-response, resilience and recovery spend relative to prevention tooling.
insights.quote: So, I think AI accelerates both tasks, but the attackers is fundamentally easier, gives them a structural advantage.

insights.claim: As AI-assisted defenses harden priority targets, adversaries are expected to adapt by shifting to softer, less-evaluated targets, with AI speeding up that displacement.
insights.speaker: Chad Sarena, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Predicts risk migration toward under-defended mid-market and municipal targets — where cyber-insurance losses and remediation demand would show up next.

insights.claim: Adversaries — nation states, non-state actors and semi-state proxies, particularly Russian-linked ones — gain an operating advantage because they are not bound by the laws, authorities and policies that constrain the US government and US tech companies.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark and Chad Sarena, Soufan Center
insights.so_what: The regulatory asymmetry argument is the standard precursor to industry lobbying for expanded private-sector defensive authorities and liability shields.

insights.claim: One intelligence official told the guests that violent non-state actors and terrorist insurgents already stay one or two steps ahead of US defenders, with growing concern that AI pushes that to three or four steps and makes the gap impossible to close.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: A stated intelligence-community view that AI uplift for low-end actors is outrunning defense — the kind of framing that drives AI-model access controls and export-style restrictions.
insights.quote: There's growing concern that AI will make that three or four steps ahead

insights.claim: Iran's tacit knowledge transfer to terrorist, insurgent and militia proxies is presented as evidence that emerging-technology capability diffuses effectively down the sophistication spectrum, extending the battlefield and keeping the United States occupied in far-flung theaters.
insights.speaker: Colin Clark, Soufan Center senior researcher
insights.so_what: Capability diffusion to proxies means sustained, geographically dispersed US operational demand — supportive of persistent defense and counter-terrorism budget lines.
